findings.summary:
The extension of the q-nomial theorem in the last paragraph needs a
stronger convergence condition when n is negative. The stated conditions
|q|<1 and |x|<1 do not suffice for arbitrary real n.

Take q=1/2, n=-1, and x=3/4. From the product definition in (40),

binom(-1,k)_q = (-1)^k q^(-k(k+1)/2),   k >= 0.

Consequently the kth term of the proposed series is

binom(-1,k)_q q^(k(k-1)/2) x^k = (-x/q)^k = (-3/2)^k.

The terms do not tend to zero. Meanwhile the finite products telescope:

product_{j=0}^N (1+q^j x)/(1+q^(j-1) x)
    = (1+q^N x)/(1+q^(-1) x) -> 2/5.

All factors in this example are finite and nonzero, so neither singular
parameters nor a choice of branch is involved.

A sufficient repair is to add |q^n x|<1. More precisely, for
0<|q|<1 and a fixed value of q^n, the product is analytic on
|q^n x|<1. Its functional equation

(1+q^n x) F(x) = (1+x) F(qx),   F(0)=1,

gives exactly the coefficients in the exercise. For nonterminating
parameters the ratio of consecutive series terms tends to -q^n x.
Thus one may replace the stated |x|<1 by |q^n x|<1, or retain it and
add the latter condition. Nonnegative integral n gives a finite sum.

findings.summary:
The bilateral Vandermonde identity in the final paragraph is not valid
for all convergent instances under the iterated-limit definition of
binomial coefficients given earlier in the same answer.

Set r=s=alpha=beta=-1/2. The proposed identity becomes

sum_{k in Z} binom(-1/2,-1/2+k) binom(-1/2,-1/2-k)
    = binom(-1,-1).

For k>=1 the first factor is zero, since its denominator contains
Gamma(1-k), while Gamma(1/2) and Gamma(k+1/2) are finite. The second
factor is finite. For k<=-1 the second factor is zero and the first
is finite. At k=0 both factors equal 1. Thus the sum has just one
nonzero term and equals 1; in particular it converges absolutely.

But binom(-1,-1)=0 under the stated definition. For generic z near -1,
taking the lower-index limit w -> -1 first gives

lim_{w -> -1} Gamma(z+1)/(Gamma(w+1)Gamma(z-w+1)) = 0.

The subsequent limit z -> -1 is still zero. This also agrees with
the book's convention that a negative integral lower index gives zero.

Hence the asserted identity reads 1=0. Every coefficient in the example
is finite, and no complex power occurs, so the qualification about
choosing branches does not resolve the discrepancy. The issue is the
singular total upper index r+s=-1, together with the lower-index-first
limiting convention. Convergence alone is not a sufficient condition.

April 17, 2015 change from y>n-1 to y>=n-1, still uses Y>0 and

findings.summary:
The exponential-tail bound requires a multiplicative constant.
For n=2, X_n is uniform on {0,1}, and mu_n=sigma_n=1/2.
Thus |(X_n-mu_n)/sigma_n|=1 surely. At x=1/2 the claimed
inequality would say 1 < exp(-a/2), impossible for any a>0.

with n>=2 and x>=0. Definition 4.1 in the cited Flajolet-Soria

findings.summary:
Write S(epsilon)=sum_{k>=1} 2^(2k-1) epsilon^(2k)/(2k^2-k).
The new bound has two problems.

First, n is missing from exp(-S(epsilon)). For n=2, epsilon=1/4,
S(epsilon)<=1/6<1/4=2 epsilon^2 n, contradicting the displayed
inequality exp(-S(epsilon))<=exp(-2 epsilon^2 n).

Second, even exp(-n S(epsilon)) is not an upper bound for all p.
At epsilon=1/2 the convergent series has sum log 2. If X is
binomial with n=8 and p=1/4, then

Pr(X>=6) = 277/65536 > 256/65536 = exp(-8 log 2).

For epsilon>1/2 the series even diverges, although such epsilon
is allowed when p<1/2.

A safe repair is to keep only exp(-2 epsilon^2 n), valid for all
p. Alternatively, the stronger series bound is valid after
inserting n and restricting to p>=1/2, 0<=epsilon<=1-p.
Indeed, the usual binomial rate function D_p has

D_p''(epsilon)=1/[(p+epsilon)(1-p-epsilon)]
                >=1/(1/4-epsilon^2)=S''(epsilon)

on that restricted interval. Both functions and their first
derivatives vanish at zero, so D_p>=S>=2 epsilon^2.

findings.summary:
The expansion for Q_x(n) in the branch x<1 fails for some
negative x. For x=-4 it predicts Q_(-4)(n)=1/5+O(1/n), whereas
the exact identity printed on page 505 gives

-4 Q_(-4)(n)+R_(-1/4)(n)=n!(-4/n)^n exp(-n/4).

The alternating series for R_(-1/4)(n) lies strictly between
3/4 and 1. But n! >= (n/e)^n, so the absolute value of the
right-hand side is at least (4 exp(-5/4))^n, whose base exceeds 1.
Thus Q_(-4)(n) tends to minus infinity along even n and plus
infinity along odd n.

n! x^(n-1) exp(n/x)/n^n,

identity or by splitting

at t=-n/x. The part beyond that point equals the missing term;
the first part equals -R_(1/x)(n)/x and has the printed
algebraic expansion. The displayed expansion for R_x(n), x<1,
does not need this correction.

findings.summary:
The first stated expected running time does not match Solution 1 on
page 513. In particular, its harmonic term is 5m H_n; the displayed
program requires 7m H_n. The claimed exponentially small remainder
also does not cover the saving from stopping at a saddle point.

Here m and n are the numbers of rows and columns, H_n=sum(1/k,k=1..n),
and all mn distinct entries are uniformly permuted. Times below are
in units u and exclude the final HLT.

A row-minimum scan costs 6n+4+7K, where K counts new strict minima after
the first entry. A nonrecord entry takes 6u, while a new minimum takes
13u: DEC1, DEC2, J2Z, CMPX, JL, JG, LDX, ENT3, INC3, ST2.
Since E K=H_n-1, this is 6n+7H_n-3 on average.

Here is a precise formula that also tracks early termination. Write
B=binom(m+n,m) and P=(m+n)/B. If all rows were processed even after a
saddle was found, the mean total number D of column comparisons would
be, for n>1,

D = n(m+1)/(n-1) - (m+n)^2/((n-1)B).

To derive this, number rows i=0,...,m-1 in processing order and let
U be their minimum after replacing random ranks by independent uniform
(0,1) entries. Then a_t=E U^t=1/binom(n+t,t), and

E D_i = sum(t=0..m-1) a_(t-[i<t]),
  D = sum(t=0..m-1) ((m-t)a_t+t a_(t-1)).

The second summand at t=0 is zero. The indicator accounts for the
comparison with the row minimum itself. Summing the beta integrals
gives the displayed value of D; no independence of the D_i is needed.

The cost W_i of a completed row, including its column check and its
transition or successful return, is 6n+8+7K_i+5D_i. Therefore the actual
expected time, without HLT, is exactly

A - 5(m+n)^2/((n-1)B) - Delta,
  A = 6mn+7m H_n+6m+6+5(m+1)/(n-1).

Delta is the mean cost of the rows omitted after a saddle is found.
There is at most one saddle; each row contains it with probability
P/m. Since 6n+13 <= W_i <= 13n+5m+1, one has

(6n+13)(m-1)P/2 <= Delta <= (13n+5m+1)(m-1)P/2.

In particular, on square matrices m=n=k, the discrepancy from the
published expression has leading size 2k(H_k-1), not an exponentially
small size. Even after replacing 5m H_n+8m by 7m H_n+6m, the stated
O((m+n)^2/B) remainder is too small: the lower bound on Delta is of
order k^3/B. Both corrections to A are negative, so cannot cancel.
The exact formula and the bounds above avoid making an unsupported
claim about a sharper remainder. A safe bound is O(m(m+n)^2/B).

The second expected-time formula in the same addition is consistent
with its program when HLT is excluded; its remainder has an independent
proof in notes/mixal-saddle.md.

The relevant Hofri-Jacquet preprint was read, but its generic instruction
multipliers were not substituted for an actual MIX instruction count.
Independent finite exact expectations, direct instruction execution,
and exhaustive small matrices agree (results/mixal-saddle.json).

This is a finding about the published added answer and the displayed
program, not a claim that the saddle search is incorrect. Priority and
inspection of a physical printed copy remain unverified.

findings.summary:
"The first systematic algorithm for calculating the date of Easter"
appears too strong. The earlier canon traditionally attributed to
Hippolytus contains a table of Easter Sundays in seven columns of
sixteen years. The inscription and tables, with Latin translations,
are printed in Patrologia Graeca 10 (1857), cols. 875-884.
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.22.1, already describes the
sixteen-year paschal canon; see also PG 10, cols. 571-572.

Victorius himself discusses earlier cycles of 84, 95, and 112 years
and their repetition in his letter to Hilarius, section 3 (Mommsen,
Chronica minora I, MGH Auctores antiquissimi 9, 1892, pp. 678-679).
His own 532-year construction is described in section 10, pp. 683-684.

Reading a fixed table by year with cyclic repetition is a finite,
systematic procedure. This interpretation includes tabular canons
of the same general kind as the work attributed to Victorius.
It does not require their lunar models to be astronomically exact.
The transcription notes a damaged character in the earlier table;
the observation concerns the existence and structure of the earlier
procedure, not a new reconstruction of every inscription character.

A minimal revision would replace "The first systematic algorithm"
with "An important early systematic algorithm". This does not
assign a new absolute priority to Hippolytus or resolve the disputed
identity of all works traditionally attributed to him. A narrower
priority claim about a particular western 532-year cycle would need
separate qualification.

All four public errata layers were checked. The 2014 change from
Aquitania to Aquitaine does not address the priority claim; no
corresponding correction was found. The scan of the first printing
was directly inspected; later physical printings were not checked.
This report has not been sent or published.

findings.summary:
MAXWDS=1200 is described as the maximum input length. Both PERM and
ANS reserve MAXWDS words. However, valid nonempty input cycles can
produce a longer disjoint-cycle representation, even after singleton
cycles are removed.

Let a_1,...,a_t,b_1,...,b_t be distinct names. Under the book's
left-to-right composition convention, the product

(a_1 a_2 ... a_t)
  (a_1 b_t a_t b_(t-1) a_(t-1) ... b_2 a_2 b_1)

is (a_1 b_1)(a_2 b_2)...(a_t b_t). Indeed, the second cycle maps
b_i to a_i and a_i to b_(i-1), with cyclic subscripts. Applying the
first cycle and then the second therefore exchanges a_i and b_i.
The input has 3t+4 fields, including parentheses; the answer has 4t.

For t=320, use five-character names A0001,...,A0320,B0001,...,B0320.
The 964 nonblank input fields, blank padding, and final equals field
fit in 61 cards (976 words), well below the 1200-word limit. Every
cycle is nonempty and has distinct elements, as required. The answer
needs 1280 words.

An instruction-level MIX run reaches the first write outside ANS at
line 64, address 2400, after 2938338 instructions. It subsequently
replaces the instruction at OPEN (2458) with the name B0315 and
fails when it returns there, before printing any answer. The 61 input
cards have been echoed. This behavior is additional reproduction;
the field-count construction itself already proves the allocation
insufficient.

One conservative repair is to introduce

MAXANS EQU 2*MAXWDS+23

and change line 03 to

ANS ORIG *+MAXANS

If N is the number of distinct input names, N<=MAXWDS. A surviving
cycle with k>=2 names occupies k+2<=2k words; hence the final answer
has at most 2N words. The extra 23 words cover the terminating zero
and padding written by lines 51-52. Temporary singleton output also
fits this bound with the extra space. The all-fixed case produces
only the two parentheses. The resulting program still fits in MIX's
4000 words and its two-byte index range for every allowed byte radix.

The allocation-only repair produces the exact 1280-word answer for
the counterexample at byte radices 64 and 100, including asynchronous
I/O. Each run executes 3197486 instructions and prints 61 echo rows
plus 54 answer rows. All 37 radices assemble within memory.
This repair does not address the separate question about empty-cycle
input, recorded only as candidate V1-C0028.

No applicable correction was found in all1-prepre, all1-pre, all1,
or err1, searched by page and Program A/input/answer-space wording
on 2026-11-01. Nearby corrections concern input wording, style, or
analysis. No priority claimed. Nothing has been sent.

The same allocation problem also affects Program B, pp.174-175,
line 05 (ANS EQU PERM). It remains after the published correction
ENT3 1 -> ENT3 0. The same t=320 input reaches the first answer
write outside PERM/ANS[2400..3599] at line 60, address 3600, after
945974 instructions. This run stops BEFORE that write; no assertion
about later corrupted execution of B is needed.

Unlike A, B already reserves three 1200-word tables. One conservative
repair that fits MIX memory is to reduce MAXWDS explicitly to 960
(60 cards) and reserve 2*MAXWDS+23 words for PERM/ANS. This changes
B's declared input limit. The last occupied address is 3962. All 37
radices assemble; complete runs at 64/100 on the 60-card t=318 input
produce all 1272 answer words correctly. Preserving the original
75-card limit would require a different storage/output arrangement;
that is not claimed for this simple repair.

findings.summary:
The words "any function" need an integrability qualification. For w=1/2,
let I_n be the cycle structure of the identity and J_n that of a single
n-cycle. For n>=2, put phi(I_n)=2^n n! and phi(J_n)=-2^n n, and set phi=0
elsewhere (including sequences with infinite total size). This is a
finite-valued measurable function on the whole stated domain.

Under the uniform distribution on permutations of n objects, I_n has
probability 1/n! and J_n has probability 1/n. Hence phi_n=0 for every n,
and the displayed series converges absolutely to zero. However,
P(N=n)=2^(-n-1), so each n>=2 contributes 1/2 to each of E(phi^+) and
E(phi^-). Both are infinite, and E(phi) is undefined.

One could require E|phi|<infinity; alternatively, nonnegative functions
are allowed if infinite expectations are admitted. Convergence of the
displayed series alone is insufficient.

assumption. All four errata layers (all1-prepre, all1-pre, all1, err1)

findings.summary:
The update loop can overwrite the infinity marker of an already chosen
vertex. For four terminals take the symmetric finite costs

c14=1, c12=2, c24=3, c34=10, c23=20, c13=30.

Initially a=(1,3,10), b=(4,4,4). The first iteration chooses vertex 1
and edge 14, leaving a=(infinity,2,10). The second chooses vertex 2 and
edge 21. Its update restores a(1)=2 and b(1)=2, so a=(2,infinity,10).
The third and last iteration therefore chooses edge 12 again. Vertex 3
is disconnected. There are no ties, zero costs, or infinite input costs.
Undefined diagonal comparisons may harmlessly be omitted; the failure
does not depend on their interpretation.

Restrict the update to as-yet unchosen vertices other than i. With the
printed marking convention, require j!=i and a(j)<infinity before
testing c(i,j)<a(j). Already chosen markers then stay unchanged, while
each other a(j) remains the cheapest connection to the chosen set.
The next minimum extends that set by one vertex. The usual exchange
across this cut proves minimum total cost, and the time remains O(n^2).
The linked-list alternative in the next paragraph avoids this defect.

errata PDF pages, read the exercise's general cost contract, and checked
the three iterations and general repair. Exhaustive supplemental tests

findings.summary:
The exercise on page 377 asks for the fundamental cycles to be printed.
Steps C5-C6 explicitly print each edge of each cycle, with its sign.
Consider the input arcs, in this order,

(1,2),(2,3),...,(n-1,n), (1,3),(1,4),...,(1,n).

There are m=2n-3 arcs. The first n-1 form the accepted spanning path.
The later fundamental cycles have lengths 3,4,...,n. Their total
printed length is L=n(n+1)/2-3=Theta(n^2). Consequently the stated
O(m log n) bound cannot hold for this output contract, regardless
of improvements to connectivity bookkeeping.

The proposed DFS alternative needs the same qualification. In the
underlying fan graph, vertex 1 has degree at most three in every
DFS spanning tree: before reaching it, the DFS path is an interval
of vertices 2,...,n, leaving at most two unvisited path components.
Removing 1 from the DFS tree leaves at most three paths of sizes s_i.
Their attachment positions give

sum_{v=2}^n dist_T(1,v) >= sum_i s_i^2/4 >= (n-1)^2/12.

At most three spokes (1,v) belong to the tree. The other spokes alone
produce cycles of total length at least (n-1)^2/12+(n-1)-6.
Thus every DFS tree in this sparse family requires Omega(n^2)
explicit output. This is not a lower bound for arbitrary cycle bases:
a non-DFS star spanning tree yields short triangles.

A precise replacement is: DFS constructs a spanning tree and its
non-tree arcs in O(n+m) time, representing the cycles implicitly.
Explicitly listing these cycles requires and permits O(n+m+L) time,
where L is their total length. The original C1-C6 time claim should
be removed or replaced by a justified bound for its actual contract.

The cited Tarjan primary text constructs a compact palm tree and
fronds; it does not list all edges of all fundamental cycles.
All four errata layers were searched without a matching correction.
Physical printing and priority are unverified. No report sent externally. The November 5 sequential review reconfirmed the original location and general argument; all four refreshed errata layers still lack a repair. Accepted computations were not repeated.

findings.summary:
Exercise 23 chooses positive U and V, so the printed sine 2UV/(U^2+V^2) is always positive. With one angle per pool, uniform affine offsets and the recommended angle rejection, E(cos theta)=0 and beta=E(sin theta)=3(sqrt(3)-1)/pi.

Take the first 682 X entries from each 2048-entry pool and divide their sum by sqrt(682). This uses the suggested one-third of the pool. The expected update matrix has off-diagonal blocks beta*J and -beta*J, where J averages 1024 coordinates. Two independent passes therefore give covariance -(682/1024)*beta^2 = -0.325469... .

The printed positive scale is a=abs(Y_1023+sqrt(4095))/sqrt(2*S). Exact Gaussian and spherical moments bound the change in covariance by less than 0.1, proving scaled covariance below -0.22. The proof includes rare negative values inside the absolute value and does not replace S by its mean.

An independent random sign on the sine removes this particular mean-matrix mechanism. It does not prove independence or eliminate every finite-pool defect. The conclusion concerns the explicit common-angle recipe and output schedule; Brent’s implementation changes matrices within a pass.

The complete proof, code, four archived result blocks, original page and all errata layers were reviewed again on November 6, 2026 without rerunning the experiments. Brent’s later paper already discusses the general need for random signs. No corresponding correction to this answer was found in the available errata. The latest physical printing and novelty remain unverified.

findings.summary:
The displayed probabilities of the inner and outer boxes need clipping.
As printed, the equalities need not hold for all the bases b_j.

For the inner equality, take k=2, b=2, u_1=u_2=0, v_1=v_2=1/4.
Then u'_i=v'_i=0. The inner event requires 1/2 <= U < 0 in each
coordinate, so its probability is 0. The printed product is instead
(-1/2)^2=1/4. For the outer equality, k=1, u=0, v=1, b=2 gives
Pr(0 <= U_n < 3/2)=1, whereas the printed length is 3/2.

The theorem remains true. One repair is to use

inner_i = [ceil(b*u_i)/b, floor(b*v_i)/b),
  outer_i = [floor(b*u_i)/b, ceil(b*v_i)/b),

interpreting the inner interval as empty if its endpoints are reversed.
The correct volumes are

product_i max(0, floor(b*v_i)/b - ceil(b*u_i)/b),
  product_i (ceil(b*v_i)/b - floor(b*u_i)/b).

All endpoints lie in [0,1]. These boxes sandwich the target box,
and their volumes converge to product_i(v_i-u_i) as b tends to infinity.

findings.summary:
The count of changed k-tuples needs a factor depending on k. Replacing
U_(j^2) by zero can change up to k overlapping windows per changed term,
so the printed bound sqrt(n) is not valid for k-tuples.

For example, take k=2, n=16, and U_0,...,U_16=3/4, followed by any
completely uniformly distributed tail. Before the replacement, all
16 pairs starting at indices 0,...,15 lie in [1/2,1)^2. Afterwards the
pairs starting at 0,1,3,4,8,9,15 no longer do: seven changes, exceeding
sqrt(16)=4. Even if only pairs wholly inside the first 16 terms were
counted, there would be six changes.

A safe bound for n starting positions is

k * (1 + floor(sqrt(n+k-2))).

After division by n this tends to zero for every fixed k, so the main
conclusion, that complete uniform distribution is preserved, is correct.
Replacing 'at most sqrt(n)' by 'O(k sqrt(n)) for fixed k' suffices.

findings.summary:
The suggested use of Algorithm W gives the opposite prefix inequality.
W6 increments the counter from zero to k=1 before returning V_k, so
U_0=V_1=1/2. Thus the number of the first one terms strictly below 1/2

findings.summary:
The auxiliary assertion that U_(s_N) lies in a block B[a_1,...,a_t]
with t <= q+1 is false under the stated choice of q.

Let every subsequence rule select every term, and take r=q=1, N=16.
Then 4^r <= 4^q < N <= 4^(q+1), as required. The block B[1] emits
3 terms, and B[1,1] emits the next 12. Hence U_15 and U_16 are in
B[1,1,1]. In particular U_(s_N)=U_16 has depth 3, not at most 2.
The same issue occurs for N=4^(q+1) for every q>=1.

This is a local problem in the proof, not a counterexample to Theorem W.
For a fixed prefix of length r, reaching depth t requires that its
ancestor blocks at depths r,...,t-1 have already been filled. Their
combined capacity is 4^(t-1)-4^(r-1). Thus t <= q+2 is safe. Using
this weaker bound, and explicitly accounting for the finitely many
ancestor outputs, gives a discrepancy bound

4/sqrt(N) + O_r(1/N),

which still proves the theorem. This does not assert that the final
constant 2 printed in the book is itself false; the issue is the stated
auxiliary justification for the block count.

findings.summary:
The stated uniqueness of the sequence of points is false. Reflection
preserves every gap length. Put

W_n = lg(2n+1) mod 1,
  Z_0 = 0, and Z_n = 1-W_n for n >= 1.

For n >= 1, W_n is strictly between 0 and 1, since the odd integer
2n+1 is not a power of two. Thus Z is also an admissible [0..1)
sequence starting at zero. For every n, the first n points of Z have
exactly the same multiset of gaps as the first n points of W. Both
therefore satisfy all the stated inequalities, with equality.
Nevertheless W_1=lg(3/2), whereas Z_1=lg(4/3).

A possible correction is to assert that every sequence satisfying the
inequalities has the same sorted gap lengths as W, for every n. The
unique object is the sequence of gap multisets, not the point sequence.
This agrees with Theorem 2 in Ramshaw's original Stanford report
CS-TR-77-637 (1977), whose strategies are defined in terms of lengths.
The minimax conclusion in part (c) is unaffected.

findings.summary:
The proposed initial boundary a_0=s_0 need not start an increasing
sequence of boundaries. For the admissible computable injection s_j=j,
the recurrence

a_(m+1) = max{s_j : 0<=j<2^(a_m)}

most a_m+1 elements. R5 therefore implies that the proportion of ones

zero without fraction overflow and without any normalization shifts.
The modified routine executes three additional unit-time instructions:

instruction costs. Thus the running time increases by 3u; it does not
decrease by 3u. For equal fractions +1/b and -1/b with exponent QQ, the
complete times are 60u and 63u. The 2012 correction from line 22 to line 23
has been applied.

It need not be the total increase. With b = 100 and both exponents QQ,
use positive fractions U/b^8 and V/b^8, where

The original product is just below 1/b; the modified product is exactly
1/b. The modification costs 2u before DNORM but saves a 6u normalization
iteration, so total time decreases from 112u to 108u.

changes in the normalization path. In answer 5 the extra cost before

one normalization iteration is not universal.

findings.summary:
The displayed choice of r in Newman's construction does not give the
stated upper bound. The bound itself remains valid after changing r.

Write t=ln(m), u=ln(t), and a=(ln(2))^2/2. The printed choice

r=floor((1+ln(2)/(2*lg(lg(m))))*ln(m)/ln(ln(m)))

satisfies r=(t/u)(1+a/u+O(1/u^2))+O(1). Using the expansion for p_r
cited in the answer and k=p_1*...*p_r gives

ln(k)=t+(a-1)*t/u+O(t*ln(u)/u^2).

Thus the number of multiples of k that the construction explicitly
computes is

floor(m^2/k)=m*exp((1-a+o(1))*ln(m)/ln(ln(m))).

Since a<1, this is much larger than m, whereas the claimed chain has
length m+o(m). This is an asymptotic obstruction, not a choice of the
implicit constant. Merely changing lg lg m to ln ln m is insufficient.

One valid replacement is

r=floor((1+(1+ln(2)/2)/ln(ln(m)))*ln(m)/ln(ln(m))).

Then ln(k)=t+(ln(2)/2)*t/u+O(t*ln(u)/u^2). Both m^2/k and the
precomputation bound 2^(-r)*k*ln(k) have logarithm

t-(ln(2)/2)*t/u+O(t*ln(u)/u^2),

which proves the stated upper bound for every fixed epsilon>0.

For a finite illustration, m=2^1024 gives printed r=111 and p_r=607.
The exact primorial has 831 bits; floor(m^2/k) has 1218 bits.

I checked all six available errata layers, including the older
second-edition amendment dated 1997-06-28, p. 638, answer 33, line 8,
which changes (1+ln(2)/2) to ln(2)/2. That amendment does not supply
the above correction to the formula printed in the third edition.
Without the original second-edition page I am not identifying which
occurrence it changed. No matching third-edition correction was found.

findings.summary:
The endpoint optimization of J1--J4 saves two divisions, rather than
one multiplication and one division (for n >= 2).

Put m=floor(n/2), h=ceil(n/2). The stated unoptimized counts,
n+h-1 multiplications and n divisions, are correct. At the upper
endpoint, restore u_n instead of dividing the scaled v_n by x_0^h.
At the lower endpoint, replace

x_0^m * (u_0/x_0^m + w)

by u_0 + x_0^m*w, where w is v_1 just before the j=0 operation.
This removes the initial division but leaves the multiplication.
Thus the improved counts are n+h-1 multiplications and n-2 divisions.

The printed allocation is impossible in general already for n=2:
it would give one multiplication and one division. The required
constant coefficient u_0+u_1*x_0+u_2*x_0^2 has total degree three
in the input coefficients and x_0. A straight-line program with
one multiplication, one division, and arbitrarily many additions
has growth at most quadratic under generic simultaneous scaling
of all inputs. If multiplication comes first, the division has
polynomial operands of degree at most two. If division comes first,
its affine operands give a quotient growing at most linearly,
and the subsequent multiplication gives at most quadratic growth.

Two multiplications and no divisions do suffice for n=2:

b = u_2*x_0;
    w = u_1+b;
    v_0 = u_0 + x_0*w;
    v_1 = w+b;
    v_2 = u_2.

Suggested replacement: For n >= 2, two divisions can be saved by
treating v_n and v_0 as special cases. For n=1, only one division
can be saved.

The total saving of two multiplication/division operations remains
valid for n >= 2; the algorithm's computed values are correct.

page_map.coordinate_note: One segment per file page, including frontmatter. Printed labels are shown where mapped.
page_map.coverage_note: Green: Reviewed under the agreed printed-argument standard, with explicit exceptions in the details. Gray: Not reviewed. Red markers identify audit-supported errors independently of coverage. Published errata are excluded. Review checks the printed text, exercises and answers together; it does not require new proofs of standard results or solutions to open research problems.

progress.methodology: One reviewer checks the printed text, exercises and answers together. Existing sound work is reused. Standard theorems are accepted; new proofs, open research problems and disproportionately expensive reproductions are outside the agreed scope. Exact exceptions are recorded. Coverage has two states: Reviewed and Not reviewed. Red finding markers are independent of coverage. Known errata are excluded from findings.

classification_note: Severity is a provisional impact rating. All 806 baseline-confirmed cards were rechecked for correctness and prior publication on November 12, 2026. Retained findings have no matching prior report in the checked sources; absolute priority is not established. Your personal review is separate.
